title: Benefits of the AWS Cloud
learningObjective: Distinguish scalability, elasticity, high availability, fault tolerance, and agility in exam scenarios.
summary: The cloud offers global reach, high availability, elasticity, and agility: you provision resources in minutes and pay per use, without buying hardware.
explanation:
Imagine that instead of buying a building for your business, you rent a space in any city in the world and pay only for the days you occupy it. That is what the cloud does with technology infrastructure.

AWS has Regions (sets of data centers) on several continents. From the console, you can create a server in minutes in any Region, without buying or installing anything physical: that is agility and global reach.

Two concepts are often confused. Scalability is being able to handle more load by adding resources. Elasticity goes further: adjusting them automatically in both directions — growing when demand rises and shrinking when it falls. High availability means the system keeps operating even if part of it fails (for example, running the application across multiple Availability Zones). Fault tolerance goes beyond that: the system keeps working correctly despite failures. And disaster recovery (DR) is the strategy for recovering from a severe failure, sometimes by replicating to another Region.
examRelevance: Task 1.1 explicitly asks you to distinguish scalability, elasticity, high availability, resiliency, agility, and fault tolerance. Questions are usually scenarios where you pick the right term.
awsExample: An online store uses AWS Auto Scaling: during Black Friday it automatically adds EC2 instances and removes them when the campaign ends, paying only for what it consumed.

keyTerms.definition: Speed to create, test, and launch changes without waiting for hardware.
Automatic capacity adjustment with demand, both up and down.
The system stays operational through partial failures (multi-AZ).
Keeping operating correctly despite component failures.

commonConfusions.difference: Scalability = handle more load with more resources; elasticity = also automatic adjustment downward.
HA minimizes interruptions; fault tolerance keeps the service working despite active failures.
Agility is speed of change/business; elasticity is capacity adjustment.

title: AWS Well-Architected Framework: the six pillars
learningObjective: Recognize the six Well-Architected pillars and match each scenario to its pillar.
examClues: pay only for what you use
summary: AWS's framework defines six pillars for designing quality workloads: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
explanation:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is like a "best practices" checklist for designing systems in the cloud. It has six pillars and the exam expects you to identify which one matches each scenario.

Operational Excellence: running and operating systems well — automating changes, documenting, learning from failures. Security: protecting data, systems, and identities. Reliability: recovering from failures and meeting availability requirements. Performance Efficiency: using the optimal computing resources for each need. Cost Optimization: eliminating waste and paying only for what is necessary. Sustainability: minimizing environmental impact (fewer idle resources, Regions with clean energy).

Study trick: when the scenario talks about money/waste → Cost Optimization; about failures and recovery → Reliability; about processes and operation automation → Operational Excellence; about the environment → Sustainability.
examRelevance: Task 1.2 requires recognizing the six pillars, their differences, and the scenarios associated with each. It is a very direct topic: learn the list and its "keyword".
awsExample: The AWS Well-Architected Tool evaluates an architecture against the six pillars and suggests improvements, such as removing idle instances (Cost Optimization).

keyTerms.definition: Each of the 6 design areas of the Well-Architected framework.
Automation, documentation, and continuous operational improvement.
Paying only for what is necessary; avoiding idle capacity.
Minimizing the environmental impact of workloads.

commonConfusions.difference: Cost saves money; Sustainability reduces environmental impact (often both at once, but the pillar is a different one).
Reliability = recovering from failures; Operational Excellence = how you run and improve the day-to-day.

title: Migrating to the cloud: AWS CAF and the 7 strategies
learningObjective: Identify a scenario's migration strategy (7 Rs) and associate responsibilities with the AWS CAF perspectives.
summary: The AWS CAF guides adoption with 6 perspectives (Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, Operations). The 7 migration strategies (7 Rs) define how to move each workload: Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Relocate, Retain, Retire.
explanation:
The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) organizes the cloud transition into six perspectives. The three business-oriented ones: Business (justifies the investment and outcomes), People (culture, leadership, training), and Governance (processes, risk, budget). The three technology-oriented ones: Platform (architecture and solutions), Security (protecting the workload), and Operations (how to run things day to day).

For moving applications, AWS describes seven strategies (the "7 Rs"): Rehost — move as is ("lift and shift", fastest). Replatform — small useful changes, such as switching the database to Amazon Aurora. Refactor/Re-architect — redesign (microservices, serverless); the most expensive but most beneficial long term. Repurchase — drop the license and buy a SaaS (e.g., a CRM as a service). Relocate — move hypervisors/hardware as is (e.g., VMware Cloud on AWS). Retain — keep it where it is for now. Retire — decommission what is no longer used.

Tricks: "no changes" = Rehost; "switch product to SaaS" = Repurchase; "change the DB engine" = Replatform; "stop using" = Retire.
examRelevance: Task 1.3 asks you to identify the migration strategy of a scenario and associate responsibilities with the CAF perspectives. It often appears as one-sentence scenarios.
awsExample: When migrating to AWS, a company replicates its VMs with AWS Application Migration Service (Rehost), converts Oracle to Aurora with SCT + DMS (Replatform), and decommissions two applications nobody uses (Retire).

keyTerms.definition: Framework with 6 perspectives for planning cloud adoption.
Switch to a different SaaS product.
Migrate with small platform changes (e.g., managed DB).

commonConfusions.difference: Nothing changes / small change (managed DB) / deep redesign.
Repurchase changes product (SaaS); Relocate moves the hypervisor/hardware as is.
CAF guides adoption (organizational perspectives); Well-Architected evaluates technical design (pillars).

title: Cloud economics
learningObjective: Apply CapEx/OpEx, economies of scale, rightsizing, and BYOL concepts to cost decisions.
summary: The cloud turns hardware investment (CapEx, fixed cost) into pay-per-use (OpEx, variable cost). Economies of scale, rightsizing, and managed services reduce total cost even further.
explanation:
Buying servers is capital expenditure (CapEx): a large upfront investment in depreciating assets. Paying for consumption on AWS is operating expenditure (OpEx): a variable cost that follows real demand. Migrating to the cloud converts CapEx into OpEx — and also eliminates hidden data center costs: power, cooling, space, physical staff.

Economies of scale is the "giant buyer" advantage: AWS aggregates the demand of millions of customers, buys hardware and power at prices impossible for a single company, and shares that efficiency.

Rightsizing is adjusting each resource to its real demand: an instance at 15% CPU is paying for air. And managed services (RDS, Lambda) reduce total cost because they remove operational work: you don't patch, you don't manage servers; and serverless models bill only for real execution, with no idle capacity.

In licensing, BYOL (Bring Your Own License) lets you reuse licenses already purchased; license-included charges the software inside the hourly price.
examRelevance: Task 1.4 asks you to compare fixed vs variable cost, recognize CapEx/OpEx, economies of scale, rightsizing, automation, and BYOL. Typical questions: scenarios of "company replaces hardware purchases with pay-per-use".
awsExample: AWS Compute Optimizer reviews your instances' real utilization and recommends smaller sizes when there is over-provisioning (rightsizing).

keyTerms.definition: Reusing your own licenses in the cloud.

commonConfusions.difference: Economies of scale = the provider's efficiency that lowers prices; rightsizing = your fine-grained resource adjustment.
CapEx = invest upfront in assets; OpEx = pay for continuous consumption.

rows.a: On-prem: you pay for unused capacity

rows.b: Cloud: included in the per-use price
Cloud: variable, measurable with Cost Explorer
